The researchers suspected that the presence of shade …
questions.passage:
Measuring the benefit of shade

A university team studying two pedestrian routes found that both had almost the same afternoon air temperature. People nevertheless described one route as much cooler. The researchers suggested that shade reduced the radiant heat reaching a walker even where the shaded and unshaded areas shared much of the same air. They added a separate instrument to estimate the thermal radiation experienced along each route.

The team first compared the two routes at noon. A maintenance worker pointed out that the busiest time was later, after a lecture ended. At that hour the shadow from a tall building had moved away from the queue at one entrance. The researchers therefore returned at several times of day to learn when the protection was actually available to people using the route.

Their observations also showed why canopy area alone can be misleading. On one street, most of the leaves were above a planted strip inside a fence. Passers-by had to walk on the exposed outer pavement. Another street had fewer trees, but their crowns extended over the line pedestrians usually followed.

For the final report, the team marked shaded stretches alongside unshaded waiting areas on a map. The aim was to help planners find places where people stood outdoors for several minutes, even if those places accounted for only a small proportion of the total walkway.

Sentence endings
A. helps planners identify exposed waiting locations
B. does not show whether people walk beneath the canopy
C. allowed the team to compare the maturity of the trees
D. could miss the conditions when most pedestrians used the route
E. could influence how much radiant heat reached a person
F. allowed the team to prove one street always had cooler air
questions.explanation: Could influence how much radiant heat reached a person. The first paragraph distinguishes radiant exposure from air temperature.

The first transcription of the interviews …
questions.passage:
Indexing the spoken record

A town archive acquired interviews with people who had worked at a railway depot. The first transcription pass was produced quickly because the archivists chiefly wanted a search aid. Searching a phrase could take a user to roughly the right passage, but many names were spelled inconsistently. For that reason the archive asked researchers to check names against the recording and other records before citing them.

A second difficulty arose when speakers referred to buildings that no longer existed. Several used the same informal nickname for different buildings. To help listeners, a volunteer team produced a map from old plans and added approximate dates to each location. The combination helped distinguish a nickname used in the 1950s from the same name applied to a later building.

Some interviews included long pauses. An editor suggested cutting them so the recordings would be easier to browse. The archive retained the originals but created short excerpts for visitors who wanted a quick introduction. Researchers could therefore hear a whole answer in context, while casual visitors could still sample the collection.

The archivists eventually invited former depot workers to suggest corrections. When people offered conflicting interpretations, the staff left both suggestions visible with a short explanation of the disagreement. This approach allowed new information to improve the index while preserving evidence that later researchers might weigh differently.

Sentence endings
A. captured the precise spelling of every name
B. explained why listeners should ignore long pauses
C. offered a choice between quick access and full context
D. helped locate a passage without settling every spelling
E. helped date and distinguish places with a shared nickname
F. kept disagreements available for later evaluation
questions.explanation: Helped locate a passage without settling every spelling. It was intended for searching, and names still needed checking.
